steps.body: Different random samples of the same population usually give slightly different estimates — that's normal variation, not a mistake. Bigger samples tend to vary less from each other.
Vary selection method and sample size to see two different sources of error.

widget.prompt: Estimate neighborhood recycling. Choose a representative design, use at least 100 people, and repeat the sample.
widget.successFeedback: Random selection addresses bias; the larger repeated samples reduce random variability.
widget.methodFeedback: A convenience sample can systematically overrepresent one part of the neighborhood.
widget.sizeFeedback: Random is fair, but this sample is still too small to control random variability well.
widget.drawsFeedback: Run more samples to see the spread of estimates before trusting the pattern.

cml.actionGoal: Experiment with method and size as separate levers on sampling quality.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Make the sample ten times larger without changing a biased method. Which problem remains?

explanation.prompt: Why can a very large convenience sample still be misleading?

options.label: It can repeatedly overrepresent the same easy-to-reach group.
options.feedback: Exactly — size cannot repair a biased selection process.

options.label: Large samples are always accurate.
options.feedback: Large samples can be precisely wrong when selection is biased.

options.label: Repeat the same biased selection many times.

predict.reveal: A larger sample reduces random variability, but only representative selection addresses systematic bias.

steps.body: Identify which sample would vary less.
explanationVariants: A bigger random sample tends to give more consistent, reliable estimates.
More data points smooth out random chance swings.

widget.prompt: Which random sample is likely to give a MORE RELIABLE estimate of a school's average test score?

options.label: A random sample of 200 students
options.feedback: Yes — a bigger random sample tends to vary less from the true population value.

options.label: A random sample of 10 students
options.feedback: A small sample can swing widely just by chance — less reliable than a bigger one.

options.label: Both are equally reliable
options.feedback: Sample size does matter — the bigger random sample tends to be more reliable.

steps.body: Taking several different random samples and comparing their estimates shows you how much natural variation to expect.

widget.prompt: Run repeated random samples from a population where 55% prefer pizza. Compare how the pile changes from n = 30 to n = 120.
widget.successFeedback: At n = 120 the estimates cluster more tightly around 55%. Larger random samples reduce sampling variability.
widget.wrongSizeFeedback: This sample size still produces a wider pile. Increase n and compare the spread.
widget.moreDrawsFeedback: Run more samples before judging the spread; a handful of dots is not a distribution.

steps.body: Scaling works the same no matter the sample size — the math doesn't change, only how confident you can be in the result.

widget.prompt: In a sample of 80 people, 20 have visited the new museum. If the city has 3200 people, estimate how many have visited.

commonErrors.feedback: That's just the sample count. Scale it up: 20/80 of 3200 = 800.
That's everyone, not just museum visitors. Scale the ratio: 800.

explanationVariants: A bigger random sample gives a more reliable, less variable estimate.
More data smooths out chance swings.

widget.prompt: Which random sample is likely to give a MORE RELIABLE estimate of a city's average commute time?

options.label: A random sample of 500 residents
options.feedback: Yes — a bigger random sample tends to vary less from the true value.

options.label: A random sample of 15 residents
options.feedback: A small sample can swing widely just by chance — less reliable.

options.label: Both are equally reliable
options.feedback: The bigger random sample tends to be more reliable.

explanationVariants: Scale the sample's ratio up to the full population.

widget.prompt: In a sample of 40 workers, 16 bike to work. If the company has 600 workers, estimate how many bike to work.

commonErrors.feedback: That's just the sample count. Scale it up: 16/40 of 600 = 240.
That's everyone, not just bikers. Scale the ratio: 240.

explanationVariants: Tight clustering across several samples suggests a reliable, consistent estimate near that value.
Small sample-to-sample differences are normal, not evidence of a problem.

widget.prompt: Five random samples of 100 shoppers each estimate a store's discount-card usage rate at 41%, 39%, 42%, 40%, 41%. What's the best conclusion?

options.label: The true rate is likely close to 41%, with normal sample variation
options.feedback: Yes — five samples clustering tightly around 41% strongly suggests the true rate is near there.

options.label: The sampling method must be flawed since the numbers aren't identical
options.feedback: Small variation between random samples is expected and normal, not a flaw.

options.label: You need at least 10 more samples before concluding anything
options.feedback: Five closely-clustered samples already give a strong, useful estimate.

hints: Look at how close together the five estimates are.
That points to a true rate near 41%, not a flawed method.

steps.body: Bigger random samples tend to give more reliable estimates, and repeated sampling reveals how much natural variation to expect.
takeaways: Different random samples naturally give slightly different estimates.
Bigger samples tend to vary less and give more reliable estimates.
Tightly clustered estimates from several samples suggest a reliable true value.
